overview: This is the modern Republic of Uzbekistan, independent since 31 August 1991, not the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic and not every earlier empire centred on Samarkand or Bukhara. The atlas begins only in 1994, leaving a three-year statehood gap, and supplies three simplified shapes ending in 2020. Its outline includes Tashkent, Samarkand, Nukus and the Ferghana Valley, but leaves Termez just outside and reaches unrealistically far into neighbouring territory in the northwest; it is not a border survey. Soviet institutions and much older Silk Roads heritage are important antecedents, clearly labelled below. The republic continues after the map’s last geometry. Daily life also differs across regions, languages, generations, city neighbourhoods, farms and families, so living traditions are examples rather than rules for every Uzbekistani person.

periods.title: Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic
periods.summary: The Uzbek SSR was formed during Soviet national delimitation in 1924 and belonged to the USSR; it was an institutional predecessor, not the independent republic shown by this card.

periods.title: Independence and the Karimov presidency
periods.summary: Independence was proclaimed on 31 August 1991, UN membership followed in 1992, and Islam Karimov dominated the presidency until his death in September 2016.

periods.title: Mirziyoyev transition and reform
periods.summary: Shavkat Mirziyoyev took office in December 2016 and launched economic and administrative reforms; international observers continued to report severe limits on political competition.

periods.title: A continuing republic with unfinished change
periods.summary: Uzbekistan remains a continuing state pursuing public-service and economic changes while facing environmental, inclusion and political-pluralism challenges.

sections.title: From a Soviet republic to an independent state

items.text: The Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic was created in 1924 through Soviet national delimitation and belonged to the USSR. Tashkent became its capital in 1930. Those institutions, borders and infrastructure shaped the later country, but the Uzbek SSR was not an independent Republic of Uzbekistan and should not be quietly counted as one.

On 31 August 1991, the republic’s Supreme Soviet adopted a declaration and constitutional law on state independence and renamed the Uzbek SSR the Republic of Uzbekistan. The next day, 1 September, became Independence Day. The atlas starts in 1994, so its first shape arrives about three years late; statehood did not begin when the geometry file happened to begin.

Uzbekistan joined the United Nations on 2 March 1992. That date is a useful international marker of the new state, but independence did not erase older communities or cultures. People carried forward languages, family networks, schools, farms, industries and environmental problems from the Soviet period and from much deeper history.

Islam Karimov led the country for roughly twenty-five years after independence. When he died in September 2016, Prime Minister Shavkat Mirziyoyev became acting president and won the 4 December election, taking office on 14 December. OSCE observers described a political system with power concentrated in the presidency and little genuine competition, so the orderly succession was not the same thing as an open contest.

From 2017, the government loosened foreign-exchange controls and began restructuring prices, state enterprises and social support as part of a shift toward a market economy. The World Bank supported parts of this programme. These were real policy changes, but reform is a process: it can create new opportunities while also raising prices, displacing old jobs and leaving state dominance unfinished.

Political change remained limited. After the 27 October 2024 parliamentary election, OSCE observers said legal revisions had made some technical changes but voters still lacked genuine choice in a constrained political environment. That is a dated observer judgment, not a claim that every institution or citizen behaves alike. It belongs beside economic reform so “reform” does not become an all-purpose gold star.

A real sample of modern written Uzbek appears in Article 4 of the 2023 Constitution: “O‘zbekiston Respublikasining davlat tili o‘zbek tilidir.” It means, “The state language of the Republic of Uzbekistan is Uzbek.” This is contemporary Uzbek in the official Latin alphabet. The same article says the state respects the languages, customs and traditions of all nationalities and ethnic groups.

sections.title: Inherited brilliance, new discoveries and an environmental warning

items.text: Samarkand has been a crossroads for more than 2,500 years. In the fifteenth century, Ulugh Beg’s scholarly court built a huge observatory and compiled influential star tables with mathematicians including al-Kashi. One surviving instrument was built into the ground at monumental scale. This was a collaborative Timurid achievement centuries before modern Uzbekistan, not something the 1991 republic can claim to have invented.

Modern archaeology sometimes begins in orbit. Since 2008, researchers have compared declassified CORONA spy photographs with ASTER, Landsat and commercial satellite images to spot old roads, canals and settlements in Uzbekistan. NASA reported dozens of candidate sites, followed by work on the ground. Fun fact: a Cold War camera can become an archaeology tool, but a suspicious pixel is a clue, not a discovery until researchers check it.

The Aral Sea disaster is an inherited Soviet-era warning about giant engineering schemes. River water was diverted to irrigate crops, especially cotton, and the sea shrank dramatically. Roughly 60,000 square kilometres of exposed seabed became the salty, dusty Aralkum Desert. Winds can carry salt and pollutants toward farms and homes, turning a distant-looking shoreline change into a daily health and livelihood problem.

Uzbekistan and its partners are planting and restoring vegetation on degraded land to hold soil and reduce dust. A 2025 World Bank brief reported 500,000 hectares under afforestation. That is a large area, about 700,000 football pitches, but “trees planted” is not the same as “the Aral Sea restored.” Survival, species choice, water use and long-term monitoring still matter.

sections.title: Palov, punchlines, dancing and family care

items.text: Palov combines rice with meat, vegetables and spices, but its social job is as important as its recipe. It is prepared for guests, weddings, New Year, memorials and help for people in need, and skills pass through families and apprenticeships. UNESCO says guests traditionally leave only after palov is served. In kid language: leaving before the rice appears may be a tactical mistake.

Askiya is competitive comedy made from words. Performers improvise witty exchanges around a theme at festivals, family events and neighbourhood gatherings, trying to answer quickly without becoming cruel. The tradition has historically been practised mainly by men, according to UNESCO. Good askiya rewards observation and timing: think verbal table tennis, except the ball is a punchline and nobody gets to ask for five minutes to write a comeback.

Khorazm’s Lazgi dance uses music and movement to express love, happiness and the natural world. At weddings and community celebrations, spectators may join the performers voluntarily. That makes the border between “audience” and “dancer” delightfully unsafe: standing too close to the dance floor may result in becoming part of the show. It is a regional living tradition, not a dance every Uzbekistani person performs.

In Margilan, artisans make atlas and adras ikat fabrics by binding and dyeing threads before weaving. A community centre founded in 2007 helped masters teach apprentices and document techniques that had weakened during industrial standardization. The fuzzy-edged patterns are planned before the cloth exists, rather like colouring individual strands and then solving a beautiful loom-sized puzzle.

Families often do unseen work when public services are inaccessible. Bakhriddin Choriev moved to Tashkent and rearranged employment and daily travel so two of his children with disabilities could attend school and receive support; he later advocated for other families. His story is inspiring, but it also exposes a burden: inclusion should not depend on whether one parent can reorganize an entire life.

Inclusive schooling is still rare for many disabled children. In June 2026, UNICEF estimated 122,300 children with disabilities in Uzbekistan but said only 5,999, fewer than one in twenty, were enrolled in mainstream schools. A programme supported 50 model schools and asked children to express inclusion through drawings and poems. Model classrooms are a start; the numbers show the national gap remains enormous.

Nurse Umida has worked with children since 1993 and runs a vaccination room in primary care, explaining vaccines and reassuring families as well as giving injections. Her profile is a reminder that medicine is partly conversation: a calm answer can help a frightened child or parent use preventive care. One dedicated nurse, however, cannot prove equal staffing or access in every district.

A medicine-reimbursement pilot began in Syrdarya in 2022 so eligible patients could receive certain prescriptions through contracted pharmacies without paying the full price at the counter. WHO reported in 2024 that legislation aimed to expand the system nationwide by 2027. The grammar matters: “aimed to” is a plan, not proof that every pharmacy already provides every medicine for free.

Household water access looks high in national percentages but still consumes time. The 2021 to 2022 MICS found 96.8 per cent used an improved drinking-water source, yet 25.9 per cent did not have that source on their premises. It also found 17.9 per cent lacked a handwashing facility with soap and water at home, in the yard or on the plot. “Improved source” therefore does not always mean “turn on the kitchen tap.”

UNICEF also reports gaps in school toilets, menstrual-hygiene support and accessible facilities, especially between urban and rural settings. Work in Karakalpakstan improved water, sanitation and hygiene in 25 schools and 36 health facilities, reaching about 27,000 children. The funny-sounding truth is that a toilet can be education equipment: if it is unsafe, inaccessible or lacks privacy, pupils may simply stay home.

ending.text: Uzbekistan did not end when the atlas’s last geometry stopped in 2020. The independent republic founded in 1991 continues, with the same UN membership, while its institutions and policies keep changing. Recent market and public-service reforms coexist with limited political competition, unfinished inclusion, uneven water and health access and the inherited Aral crisis. Older monuments and traditions also continue through people, but they should not be confused with the birth date or achievements of the modern state.
